summary.secondary_aggregate_note: First tracked week — all conflicts are 'new' by definition. Rough directional gauge (unweighted average of severity scores): 68.6 — not authoritative, see protocol.md Section 9.

severity.note: 8.8M internally displaced, 4.5M refugees, cumulative deaths estimated 150,000-400,000; drone sieges around El Obeid put roughly half a million civilians at risk of large-scale atrocities, echoing the earlier El Fasher massacre.

coverage.global_english_note: Covered mainly by humanitarian/policy outlets (IRC, CSIS, Georgetown, migrationpolicy.org) rather than sustained mainstream front-page coverage; one source explicitly describes it as 'forgotten and neglected.'
coverage.plausible_reason: Limited journalist access, compassion fatigue after three-plus years, and competition from higher-profile conflicts (Ukraine, Gaza) for finite global news attention.

conflicts.notes: Widely regarded by conflict monitors as the world's largest displacement and humanitarian crisis; casualty range is wide and contested given restricted access.

severity.note: High-tempo attritional war continues; Russian losses estimated over 30,000/month, exceeding recruitment; casualty ratio has widened to near 8:1 in Russia's disfavor; no major territorial shift confirmed this week.

coverage.global_english_note: Extensive, continuous mainstream and wire coverage, including dedicated weekly tracking (e.g. Russia Matters 'War Report Card').
coverage.plausible_reason: Coverage broadly matches severity given the war's scale and direct stakes for NATO/Europe; slightly ahead of strict rank order due to sustained Western strategic interest.

conflicts.notes: One of the best-documented conflicts in the tracked set; casualty estimates still vary by source and side.

severity.note: JNIM and ISSP-affiliated groups sustain sieges, IEDs, drone and landmine attacks across Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger; UN recorded 2,640 conflict-related civilian deaths in a single quarter earlier in 2026.

coverage.global_english_note: Almost no sustained mainstream global coverage; visibility limited to specialist security/policy outlets (Security Council Report, CFR Global Conflict Tracker) and Wikipedia incident stubs.
coverage.plausible_reason: Difficult and dangerous reporting access, no single dramatic flashpoint event to anchor a story, and the AES states' withdrawal from ECOWAS/Western security partnerships has reduced Western outlets' on-the-ground presence.

conflicts.notes: Most underreported conflict in this week's tracked set relative to its casualty toll; no single dated in-window flashpoint identified, evidence reflects ongoing high-tempo pattern.

coverage.global_english_note: Milestone death-toll figure covered mainly by regional/specialist outlets (Irrawaddy, SBS, Manila Times) rather than sustained global front-page attention.
coverage.regional_note: Somewhat more visible in Southeast Asian press than in Western outlets.
coverage.plausible_reason: Severely restricted media access inside Myanmar and a long-running, diffuse multi-front conflict without a single clear narrative arc for global outlets to follow.

conflicts.notes: The 100,000 milestone was reported just before this reporting window (~July 1-2); treated here as established background context rather than an in-window event.

coverage.plausible_reason: Decades-long conflict fatigue and complex multi-actor dynamics (Rwanda's role, multiple militias) make for a harder story to package than a clean two-sided war.

coverage.plausible_reason: N/A this week — coverage and severity rank align.

coverage.regional_note: Extensively covered in Middle East-based outlets (e.g. Al Jazeera) with a generally more critical framing of Israeli conduct than much of the Western press.

coverage.plausible_reason: Commercial/shipping stakes (Red Sea trade routes) drive coverage more than the humanitarian toll of the underlying civil war does.

conflicts.notes: Exact date of the 16-troops/cargo-ship incident is unclear from available sourcing; a further, more clearly dated Saudi-Houthi escalation (tanker strikes, retaliatory strikes) appears to fall just after this window (~July 24-25) and will be assessed in next week's pass if confirmed.

severity.note: Sectarian violence in Suweida/southern Syria (Bedouin-Druze clashes, earlier Alawite-targeted killings) remains a live fault line in the post-Assad transition; cumulative tolls from 2025-2026 clashes exceed 1,000 dead and roughly 200,000 displaced, though this week had no single confirmed fresh flashpoint.

coverage.global_english_note: Substantial coverage from HRW, ICG, and ACLED given the post-Assad transition's high policy interest, though mainstream daily coverage has thinned since the acute phase of the clashes.
coverage.plausible_reason: Post-Assad Syria remains a high policy-interest story independent of this week's specific severity level.

conflicts.notes: Source reporting conflates distinct incidents across 2025 and 2026; casualty/displacement figures should be treated as cumulative context rather than this week's specific toll.

severity.note: No kinetic conflict; China continues an information and economic pressure campaign against Japan and a military buildup around Taiwan, including a July 6 SLBM test, but no direct engagement or casualties this week.

coverage.global_english_note: Substantial policy and mainstream coverage (dedicated weekly AEI tracking, major-outlet strategic-affairs pieces) despite zero current casualties.
coverage.plausible_reason: Coverage here tracks strategic/nuclear-stakes significance rather than current on-the-ground damage — a useful illustration that severity and newsworthiness are legitimately different things, not evidence of media distortion.

weeks.trajectory_note: This is the first tracked week, so there is no prior baseline for week-over-week movement; all ten situations are 'new' by definition and all changes/arrows are set to zero/steady accordingly. The starkest pattern in this baseline is the split between conflicts with the highest casualty tolls (Sudan, the Sahel insurgency, Myanmar, DRC) and their comparatively minimal presence in global/English-language media, versus conflicts with strong strategic or political salience (Taiwan, Gaza, Yemen's Red Sea dimension) that draw attention somewhat independent of current casualty counts. Russia-Ukraine and Haiti are the closest to proportionate coverage given their severity. None of this should be read as a claim that heavily-covered conflicts don't deserve their coverage — the point is that severity and newsworthiness are measured on different bases, and the biggest blind spots (the Sahel and Sudan in particular) are worth watching for whether coverage improves or the gap widens as these wars continue.
